A note on the expressions to be used on certain occasions

While speaking English — or in the spoken form of English — certain expressions are to be used because the English language is very formal and official. As learners and users of English it is necessary that the formal British idiom is learnt to make official deals, and transactions absolutely formal communicative and clear.

In the course of any conversation it is necessary to use the correct idiom, expression and usage without the influence of the mother tongue or vernacular, which includes manners and etiquette. You are expected to be very formal, and behave courteously with manners in any situation, especially while in group discussions etc.
On meeting a person for the first time in the day the usual greeting
Good morning Sir / Madam / Raju etc.
When you meet the same person or any other in the noon
When you meet in the evening
When you meet your friends, classmates and people of same age group, your greet them
Hello Raju / Remi, How are you?

When you meet a person for the first time or he is introduced by some common friend you say:
I’m glad to meet you. Glad to meet you sir. Nice meeting you — likewise the answer should be the same.
When you are wished by a friend ‘Hello Roy, How are you?’ Your answer should be fine, thank you, how are you?
If its an old friend you have not met for many days — you say, It’s long time since we met. How are things?
After meeting, your depart, on departing you wish your friends / master / father etc.
Good Bye! Friends. Bye – Bye friends. See you later friends – if it is night time you
Some times you may have to seek permission from your superiors.
Will you please excuse me sir. May I leave the room sir. May I answer your questions sir. (When it is not your turn)
Thanks is a very vital aspect of British manners. You say,
Thank you, Sir / Madam. That is very kind of you, Raju. I’m really grateful to you sir, for your timely help.

That’s all right, Sekar. — or — Not at all, Sekar. — or — It’s a pleasure. — or — Don’t mention it. — or — No mention please. — or — You are most welcome.

Framing question in the conservation is a very vital part of communication.
The basic form of a question are direct beginning with question markers viz. What, Where, When, Why, How.
The basic form of a question — the verb ‘be’ precedes the subject, and in other cases the subject is placed between the auxiliary and main verbs.
Are you accompanying me to see the movie?

In a conversation with a friend or in an official situation, asking straight questions may lack politeness. A friendly approach is needed in a conversation to elicit the right and desired response as shown below.
Would you mind if I called you up?
— No, not at all. Would you mind helping in the service?
— No, not at all. Would you like to have a cup of coffee?
— Yes, certainly or No Thank you. Could I speak to Dr. Roa please?
— Yes, please do so. Could you tell me your address?

A Question is generally asked for seeking information or classification. It has certain other functions as well. Some of them are as follows: Inviting — Would you like to attend the party? Request — Could you lend me your book? Offering help — Could I carry your brief case? Permission — May I come in? Suggestion — Could you change the date of the meeting?

The word order is very important in any question. Avoid translating questions from the vernacular. (The teacher may give suitable examples from the vernacular which influence the framing of questions in English and instruct the students to avoid those pitfalls in the process of a conversation to make communication exact and meaningful.) Differentiate between direct and indirect questions. Direct: Where is the market located? Indirect: Could you tell me the location of the market please?

Vocabulary is the most vital part of learning a language. As most of the learners in this course are familiar with the basic vocabulary, the areas of confusion is made clear with regards to spelling and usage. Language experts are of the opinion that every profession has its own register of vocabulary. This course aims at helping the learner pass over the intermediary stage before settling down to a profession, which has its own register.

Pronunciation is an essential part of communication of the language. Only standard pronunciation of R.P. – Received Pronunciation helps communicate in English, though there are many dialects in English and the English spoken in different parts of the world have variations and differences.

It is imperative that students in India learn the R.P. which is the standard used by the IELTS of Cambridge while recruiting candidates for higher studies, education and immigration to the countries where English is the official language.

As the duration of this course is limited, attention is drawn towards words which are often mis-spelt, misused or mispronounced. The only sure method of learning pronunciation of English is through the recognized system of phonetic symbols. But as most of the learners in this course are not likely to have knowledge of phonetics, to use such symbols in this course would be futile and pedantic. However, for the present purpose, learning pronunciation from the instructors in the class room is the only practical option available.
English words are dependent on accents — without accents words cannot be pronounced properly. Words are formed by a single speech unit known as “Syllable”.
the word “cut” has one speech unit. Based on the syllables, words are classified into different categories.
Word with one Speech Unit (Mono syllabic words)
Ace, bay, cow, god, day, five, key, may, can, end, eight, silk, age, too, go, row, come, hear, stop etc.
Words with two Speech Units or Two Syllables (Disyllabic words)
Forward, Reward, Context, Before, Nucleus, Birthday, Pattern, Entire, Assure, Assort, Captain, Tackle, Canal, Effect, Beside, About etc.
Words with three Speech Units or three Syllables (Trisyllabic words)
Bicycle, Calculate, Educate, Accident, Quarrelsome, Recommend, Understand, Entertain, Horizon, Familiar, Deliver, Elastic etc.
Words with Four Speech Units or Four Syllables (Tetrasyllabic words)
Caterpillar, Criticism, Capitalize, Melancholy, Rhinoceros, Unfortunate, Circulation etc.
Words with Five Speech Units or Five Syllables (Pentasyllabic words)
Irregular, Co-ordinator, Communicative, Anthropology, Pronunciation, Respectively etc.
Words with more than 5 Speech Units or compound words
Indefinitely, Anticipatory, Irregularity, Tiruchirappalli, Alphabetically, Particularization etc.
There are words in which some letters are not pronounced.

as ‘s’: cell, central, century, race, vice, ace, cyanide, face, pace, rice, duce
as ‘k’: cord, come, cut, clean, music, corn, court, cover, class, connect, curfew, canal, come, capsule

‘e’ is silent as in:

‘g’ is pronounced as [dʒ] (soft) as in:
germany, genuine, gypsy, gem, ginger, gentle, genetics, gypsum, gender, geography

rough, cough, laugh, etc.

‘h’ is silent as in:
hour, honour, honest, heir, heiress, exhibit, vehicle, vehement

know, knowledge, knight, knife, knee, knack, knob, knit, knock, knuckle, etc.

castle, christmas, bustle, thistle, bristle, etc.

Gender is an easy subject, well treated in most grammar books. The student should especially note the following. The feminine gender is denoted in three ways: a) by a suffix, b) by a word prefixed to another word, c) by an entirely different word.
Distinctive Sound of Birds and Animals
DISTINCTIVE NAMES GIVEN TO THE YOUNG ONES OF ANIMALS
Contagious / Infectious — If a disease is contagious it is transmitted by physical contact. An infectious disease can be communicated through the air or in water.
Dispose of / Dispense with — If you dispose of something you threw it away. If you dispense with it you do without it.
Explicit / Implicit — Explicit means stated directly, implicit means stated indirectly.
Flaunt / Flout — To flaunt something is to show it off in a shameless way. To flout is to deliberately ignore a rule or an accepted standard of behaviour.
A farm engaged in milk production
Graceful / Gracious — Graceful describes a person’s attractive bearing and ease of movement, Gracious implies kindness or courtesy from a superior.
Commissionaire / Commissioner — A commissioner is a member of a team – Police commissioner. A commissionaire is a uniformed doorman.

A sentence is a group of words that conveys meaning, with subject and a verb. In other words a group of words which gives a complete sense is called a sentence.
The country is under the grip of a drought. The Rose is a beautiful flower.
The right arrangement of words is very important otherwise the entire meaning of words is lost or misunderstood. Every Sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.
Wings fly, with their birds → Birds fly with their wings.
The brings, us, letters, postman. → The postman brings us letters.
Cup, milk drink this of. → Drink this cup of milk.
Assertive sentence or Statement — is a sentence which gives us information about something. It can be in the affirmative or it can be Negative.
Science is an interesting subject. — Affirmative I did not meet my friends yesterday — Negative
Interrogative sentence or Question — is a sentence which raises a question to get some information about something. It ends with a question mark. It can also be in the affirmative or negative.
Do you study your lessons daily?
— Affirmative Didn’t they pay their taxes on time?
— Negative Is your father buying a new car?
— Affirmative Aren’t you selling the old house?
— Negative Why doesn’t your brother come in time?
— Negative When did you come to India?
Imperative sentence — is a sentence which gives orders, makes requests or gives advice. It ends with a full stop. It may be affirmative and negative.
Bring me a glass of water (Order)
Exclamatory sentence — is a sentence that expresses some strong or sudden feeling.
What a beauty! How happily they are living!
Optative sentence — is a sentence that expresses a wish, probability or supposition.
May God help you. I wish they would be with me.
In a sentence words are labeled according to their function, it is called parts of speech. They are eight in number, Noun, Pronoun, Adjective, Verb, Adverb, Preposition, Conjunction and Interjection.
A word which tells the name of a person, place or a thing is called a noun.
There are five kinds of nouns:
Proper Noun: Names of specific person, place or a thing is known as a proper noun.
Common Noun: Names given in common to every person or thing of the same class or kind.
Collective Noun: Collection of persons or things taken together and spoken as a whole.
Army, flock, class, team, fleet, jury, family, nation, committee.
Material Noun: a noun that stands for matter or substance.
Abstract Noun: Denoting a thing which we cannot see or touch.
Truth, hope, honesty, health, courage, pain, joy, sleep, death, Bravery, sickness.

Any noun that stands for only one person or thing is said to be in Singular number. Any noun that stands for more than one person or things is said to be in Plural number.
Note: Uncountable nouns are rarely used in plural. Gold, Dust, Smoke, Furniture, Dirt, Sugar and Milk – never to be used in plural forms — always singular.
The following nouns have the same form for the singular as well as plural. Sheep: There is a sheep in the field. These sheep have no wool on them.

She gave us five dozen apples.
The fish is swimming in the pond.
He gave me a score of pencils.
He lived for four score years.
The following nouns are always used in singular: Furniture, news, scenery, innings, mathematics, physics.
The following nouns are always used in plural: Alms, Cattle, People, Scissors, Trousers, Spectacles, Riches, Clothes, Poultry, Vermal, Gentry.

He gave us many pieces of advice.
His house is built of stones.

There is a plenty of fish here. There were some red and white fishes caught. Mary has a golden hair. He has few white hairs in his beard.

A pronoun is a word used instead of a noun.
John is absent, he is ill.

Demonstrative Pronoun: this, that, these, those, and such. Distributive Pronoun: each, either, neither. Indefinite Pronoun: all, some, many, few, none, and such other. Relative Pronoun: who, which, whose, whom. Reflexive Pronoun: Myself, yourself, himself, herself. (They are also called Emphasizing Pronouns.)

This is a man. He stole my purse. → This is a man who stole my purse. This is a boy. His nature is good. → This is a boy whose nature is good. This is a pen. Jim likes it most. → This is a pen which Jim likes most. This is a house. Jack built it. → This is a house that Jack built. This is a boy. The teacher praised him. → This is a boy whom the teacher praised.
An adjective is a word used to add to the meaning of a noun.
He is an intelligent boy. Akbar was a brave king.
There are six kinds of adjectives.
Adjectives of Quantity — it answers the question “How much?”
He had much money. There is little food in the house. He wants some money. He did not eat any bread. He had sufficient bread. He ate the whole cake.
Adjective of Number — answering the question, “How many?”
All men are mortal. Many women were not there. Several men came to see the line. He had five rupees in his pocket. Some men are rich. The first boy won the prize. Most men are lazy.

Distributive Adjective — which refers to each one of a number:
Each woman carried a basket. Every word of it is true. Either pen will do. Neither boy is likely to pass.
Demonstrative adjectives — answer the question “which?”
This house is mine. That house is yours. I like these flowers. I want those apples. I hate such men. She lives on yonder hill.
Interrogative adjectives — it asks questions.
What colour is your skin?

Adjectives of quality — answer the question “what kind?”
Babur was a brave king. It was a cloudy day. He was an honest man. Calcutta is a big city. The rose is a beautiful flower.

Verb is a word which denotes an action. It tells us something about the subject.
He wrote a letter — wrote is a verb.
There are three kinds of verbs: Transitive verb, Intransitive verb, Verb of incomplete predication.
Transitive Verb: It requires an object after it to complete its sense.
I eat an apple. He sees a picture. He makes good toys.
Intransitive Verb: It does not need an object to complete its sense.
The man died. The girl slept. The sun shines. Birds fly in the air. He writes legibly.
Verbs of incomplete predication: There are verbs that do not have complete sense but require some word or words after them for this purpose — they are called verbs of incomplete predication.
A dog is an animal. She looks pretty. They are fair in their dealings. A thief always lives in fear. She became sad. He seems tired.
Present Participle, Gerund, Past Participle and Infinitive are parts of verb.

Tense is a term used in grammar to indicate the time of the action or event.
Present Tense 2. Past Tense 3. Future Tense
Each tense has four forms: Simple, Continuous, Perfect and Perfect Continuous
An action which is actually happening now or at the present moment — see, how it rains! Sit down. Get out.
A custom or habit — Cows give milk. I regularly get up by 5 a.m. We play tennis every day. He goes to temple every day.
A general truth — The sun rises in the east.
Present Continuous: Used to express an action going on at the time of speaking. The leaves are falling to the ground. The girls are dancing and singing now.

Present Perfect: Used to express an action that was over in the recent past with reference to the time of speaking. The sun has just set. He has already learnt his lesson. The train has just arrived. The queen has just arrived in time. He has grown tall.
I have lived in Chennai for 5 years (means the speaker is still living in Chennai). I lived in Chennai for 5 years (speaker no longer lives in Chennai).
Present Perfect Continuous: Shows an action that began in the past and is continuing up to the present time. I have been working for two hours. I have been ill for three days.
Simple Past: Expressing an action that takes place in the Past. I saw an elephant yesterday. My friend died last year. They left the house a week ago.
Past Continuous: Used to express an action begun and continuing in the Past. We were playing when you came. She was singing when I saw her.

Past Perfect: Used to express an action that had been completed before another was started. The train had left before I arrived. I had finished my work before you came. The rain had stopped before you arrived.

Past Perfect Continuous: When there are two actions in the past — the earlier action has been continuing for some time when the later action took place. He had been watching the TV when I visited him yesterday.
Simple Future: Used to express a future action or an event. I shall go to Chennai tomorrow. He will come here next Sunday.
Future Continuous: Used to express an action continuing at some point in the future time. We shall be singing a song. The girls will be playing football.

Future Perfect: Denotes the action will be completed in the future before another future action takes place. I shall have written my letter before he comes. You will have heard this news already. Nobody will have taken anything from you when you go home this afternoon. I hope you will have washed your face before you come into the room again.

Future Perfect Continuous: An action — whether finished or unfinished, will be in progress for some time. We shall have been playing three hours when you visit here. They will have been making preparation for the marriage for two months.

A past tense in the main clause is followed by a past tense in the subordinate clause.
She replied that she had no money with her. They found that he was dishonest.
There are two exceptions to this.
When the subordinate clause expresses a universal truth, then it will be in the present tense even if the main clause is in the past tense.
He said that all men are mortal. She said that God is love. He taught us that honesty is the best policy.
If the subordinate clause is introduced by the conjunction ‘than’, even if the main clause is in the past tense, it may be followed by a present tense in the subordinate clause.
She liked him better than she likes you. (Main clause – past tense; subordinate clause – present tense) He helped me more than he helps his own children.
A present or future tense in the main clause may be followed by any tense (present, past or future) required by the sense, in the subordinate clause.

She thinks that she works hard. She thinks that he worked well. She will think that he is present. She works hard lest she should fail. She worked hard lest she should fail. She will work hard lest she should fail.
The hunter killed the tiger – Active Voice. The tiger was killed by the hunter – Passive Voice.

In the first sentence, the subject (hunter) is the doer of the action, that is the subject is active. In the second sentence the subject (tiger) is the sufferer or receiver of the action, that is the subject is not active but passive. In the first sentence the verb ‘killed’ is in active voice. In the second sentence the verb ‘was killed’ is in the passive voice.
Simple present: The grocer sells sugar (AV) → Sugar is sold by the grocer (PV). Cats catch mice (AV) → Mice are caught by cats (PV).
Present Continuous: The farmer is tilling the land (AV) → The land is being tilled by the farmer (PV). Are they picking some flowers?
(AV) → Are some flowers being picked by them?
Present Perfect: He has written a letter (AV) → A letter has been written by him (PV). I have taken your books (AV) → Your books have been taken by me (PV).
Simple Past: He took my book (AV) → My book was taken by him (PV). Did he tell the truth?
(AV) → Was the truth told by him?
Past Continuous: He was playing football (AV) → Football was being played by him (PV). Were the farmers sowing the seeds?
(AV) → Were the seeds being sown by the farmers?
Past Perfect: The boys had eaten the cake (AV) → The cake had been eaten by the boys (PV).
Simple future: We shall finish the work by 6 p.m. (AV) → The work shall be finished by us by 6 p.m. (PV). He will hurt you (AV) → You will be hurt by him (PV).
Future Perfect: He will have closed the shop by 8 o’clock (AV) → The shop will have been closed by him by 8 o’clock (PV).
Certain verbs take two objects after them in the active voice, and in the passive voice one of the objects becomes the subject and the other is retained as object.
He gave me some apples (AV) → I was given some apples by him (PV). He taught us English (AV) → We were taught English by him (PV).
Some intransitive verbs (verbs that do not have direct objects) are used with prepositions as transitive verbs — have them in the passive voice.
All laughed at her (AV) → She was laughed at by all (PV). She agreed to my proposal (AV) → My proposal was agreed to by her (PV).
Imperative mood (Command or request): Shut the door. → Let the door be shut.
Interrogative (Question sentence): When did you write this letter?
→ When was this letter written by you?
Passive voice without “by”: They elected him as king (AV) → He was elected as king (PV). They named their son Samuel (AV) → Their son was named Samuel (PV).

Adverbs are used to modify verbs.
Adverb of Manner — wisely, well, fast, bravely, badly and slowly. (Answers the question HOW?)
Adverb of Place — outside, inside, everywhere, anywhere, here, there, hither and thither, forward and backward. (Answers the question WHERE?)
Adverb of Time — today, tomorrow, yesterday, daily, early, presently, immediately and ago. (Answers the question WHEN?)
Adverb of Number — twice, always, often, seldom and once. (Answers the question HOW OFTEN?)
Adverb of Degree — very, quite, nearly, entirely and partly. (Answers the question HOW MUCH?)
Interrogative Adverbs — when, where, how and why.
Noun clause — Does the work of a noun in a complex sentence.
Subject of the verb: What she says is quite true. That he is an honest man is quite clear. Why she left is a mystery.
Object of the verb: I do not know when she will come. Tell me why you told a lie.
Object of a preposition: Pay careful attention to what he says. He was greatly pleased with what I said. No one knows how old she is.
Complement of a verb of incomplete predication: Her fear is that she may fail. Life is what we make of it. His belief is that ghosts can talk.
Apposition to a noun or pronoun: My hope is that you may pass. It is clear that he was innocent. The report that he was killed is false.

Adjective clause — It is introduced by a relative pronoun or relative adverb.
This is the boy who won the first prize. This is the house that John built. The time when the train leaves is not known. The reason why he told a lie is not known.
Adverb Clause of time — Introduced by subordinating conjunctions — when, whenever, while, before, after, since, till, as etc.

When the cat is away the mice are at play. He goes mad whenever he comes to visit his mother’s grave. Do not talk while you are eating. Before you leave switch off the light. I have been ill since you have left. As soon as the train had left, my friend rushed into the platform. No sooner did he see me than he took to his heels.
Adverb Clause of place — Introduced by subordinating conjunctions — where, wherever, whenever.
I have kept the book where no one can find it. Wherever he goes follow him. You can come whenever you like.
Adverb Clause of purpose — Introduced by subordinating conjunctions — because, as, then, that and since.
I am glad because you are in time. I am glad that you do not like it. I am glad since you promise to serve me faithfully. I am glad as the truth comes out.
Adverb Clause of condition — Introduced by subordinating conjunctions — if, whether and unless.
If it rains we shall not play. He will not pass whether he works or not. Unless he works very hard he will fail.
Adverb clause of Result — Introduced by subordinating conjunctions — so.
He is so old that he can hardly work. She is so kind a woman that all respect her. The news is so good that it cannot be true.
Degree: She is younger than she looks. He is as foolish as he is lazy. He is not as wise as you think. Manner: She does as she pleases. As you sow, you will reap. It all ended as we expected.
Adverb Clause of supposition or contrast — Introduced by subordinating conjunctions — though, even though, although etc.
Though he is fair, she hates him. Although he was ill, he attended the class. Even if he is old, he is able to do a lot of work.
A preposition is a word placed before a noun or pronoun to show what relation the person or thing denoted by the noun stands to something else.
There is a cow in the field. He is fond of tea.
Simple prepositions: At, by, for, off, in, with, on, out, to, through, from…
Compound prepositions: According, above, about, along, amidst, among, around, behind, beside, between, inside, outside, underneath, within, without.
Phrase prepositions & phrasal verbs: According to, in addition to, in place of, along with, in case of, in regard to, because of, in course of, in spite of, by dint of, in favour of, instead of.
The uses of at and in
At is used for a point of time as — He came here at day break, at sunset etc. At is also used with reference to space, for small towns, villages — I met him at Keeranur. I will see him at school.
In is used for a period of time in which something happens — in the morning, in the month of May, etc. In is also used for big towns, cities, countries — He works in Mumbai. He works in Dubai.

a, an, and the are called Articles. Their function in any statement or sentence is purely grammatical.
Indefinite article: a, an. Definite article: the.
The indefinite article “a” is used before: Noun beginning with the sound of a consonant.
A boy, a flower, a woman, a cow, a horse. Such words as have the sound of (Y).
A useless person, a ewe, a European, a unit, a utensil, a unicorn, a union, a university. Nouns beginning with (O) though a vowel, but with the sound (WO).
A one rupee note, a one way road, a one eyed giant, such a one.

The indefinite article “a/an” is also used:
Idiomatically — a few, a little.
In figurative expressions — few, little.
Before numerical expressions — a lot, a thousand, a dozen.
In expressions of price, speed, ratio — 50 kms an hour, three times a day and Rs.100 a meter.
In exclamations before singular countable nouns — What a hot day! What a pretty baby!
With a noun complement, including names of professions — He is a Teacher. She is a dancer. I am an engineer.

‘The’ is a definite article. It is used:
When we refer to some particular person or thing — a) The house I have just bought is spacious. b) Call the boy wearing the blue shirt.
When a singular noun is used to indicate a class — representative in nature. c) The cow is a useful animal. d) The dog is a faithful animal.
Before rivers, ranges of mountains and group of islands — The Ganges, The Thames, The Himalayas, The British Isles, and The Andamans.
Before the ocean, seas, gulfs, bays — The Indian Ocean, The Red Sea, The Arabian Sea, The Bay of Bengal, and The Persian Gulf.
Before names of some countries, some provinces in India — The USA, The UK, The Deccan and The Punjab.
Before the names of certain well known books — The Bible, The Bagavat Gita, The Kuran.
Before adjectives in the superlative degree — May is the hottest month of the year.
When the double comparative of an adverb is used — The higher you go the colder it becomes.
Before an adjective used as a noun — The poor depend on the rich. The wise don’t like the company of foolish.
Before the names of ships, trains, hotels, theatres, clubs, etc. — The Vaigai express, The Taj Hotel, The Sapphire theatre and The INS Virat.

A question tag is a short question attached to a statement. The fundamental role of a question tag is to draw attention to the statement or to add to it. Question tags are commonly used in conversations, for emphasis and to evoke the right response from the listener.
Tag questions are always used in contraction form — aren’t, isn’t, didn’t, won’t etc.
The subject of a tag question is never a noun but a pronoun. Isn’t he?
Tags are never used with questions but added only at the end of statements. He is clever, isn’t he?
The verb in the question tag is either the auxiliary used in the statement or the proper forms of Do, Does or Did.
An affirmative statement takes a negative tag and a negative statement is followed by a positive tag. The boy is neat, isn’t he?
(Negative tag) The boy is not neat, is he?
There is always a comma between the statement and the question tag and the question ends with a question mark.

Once there lived an old lady. She became blind. She called a doctor. She agreed to pay a large fee if she got cured, but nothing if the doctor failed in his duty. The doctor attended on her. He became greedy after seeing the lady’s furniture, and delayed the cure. Every day he took away some of the furniture. At last he cured her. Then he demanded his fees. But she refused to pay him, saying that her cure was not complete. She brought a court charge on the doctor. The judge asked the lady why she would not pay the doctor. She said that her sight was not properly restored as she could not see all her furniture. The judge gave a verdict in her favour.
What had happened to the old lady?
Why did the doctor delay the treatment?
What did he do in her home?

A jackal wanted to eat crabs found on the other side of a river. It wondered how to get across the river. It then approached a camel and persuaded the camel that there were a lot of sugarcane fields on the other side of the river. The camel became very eager to taste the sugarcane and it was ready to carry the jackal across the river in return for the information it got from the jackal. The camel carried the jackal on its back and crossed the river. After having had its meal of crabs on the other side of the river, the jackal started howling. The villagers rushed out of the place and saw the camel in the sugarcane field. They beat it with sticks. The camel rushed to the river to save its skin. The jackal jumped on its back while crossing; the camel asked the jackal why he played such a trick on him. The jackal replied that it was his habit to howl after a good meal. For this the camel replied that it was his habit to take a bath after a good meal. Then he rolled in the river. The jackal was nearly drowned.
Why did the jackal want to go to the other side of the river?
What was the trick the jackal played on the camel?

Once an ant, who had come to drink at a stream, fell into the water and was carried away by the swift current. She was in great danger of drowning. A dove, perched on a nearby tree, saw the ant’s danger and dropped a leaf into the water. The ant climbed on to this and was carried to safety.

Having recognized that corruption affects human rights and the rule of law, it is important for the NHRC to develop the right to corruption-free governance, through a number of rights-based strategies in India. Rights-based approaches to governance are those strategies that rest on the conceptual foundation that social and economic goals do not remain policy objectives, but get transformed into rights that are vested with the citizenry — increasing incentives for public vigilance. In this conception there are “right-bearers” and “duty-holders” — the people will have rights relating to various social and economic goals that were hitherto described as policy objectives. The representatives of the government are vested with the duty of ensuring the protection and promotion of the particular right.

Throughout her life Mother Teresa remained humble, simple and in many senses an ordinary woman. Yet she led one of the most extraordinary lives of the twentieth century. She was not erudite, but her distilled wisdom was as profound as that of any philosopher-saint. She believed in taking one small step at a time, yet she handled several complex activities simultaneously in many parts of the world. She gratefully acknowledged the millions in donations and bequests that made her work possible, but remembered only the ‘sacrifice’ money, like that of the little Calcutta boy who ate no sugar for three days to offer her one rupee that was thus saved. Although she lived and worked in largely Hindu India, she made no attempt at conversion. Conversion, she said, was God’s work, not hers. In reflecting this position, she also astutely conformed to her environment, while at the same time being faithful to Jesus, whom she saw in all those whom she ministered to and encountered.

4. ARE WOMEN MORE DEPENDENT ON RELATIONSHIPS FOR IDENTITY?

Most studies show that women have more difficulty establishing their singularity than men. The old stereotype is that men live for their work and women live for love; hence, when a relationship ends, a divorce occurs, or a friendship blows up, it is harder on women than on men.

Does that mean that women are by nature weaker and more dependent? Not at all. It has to do with the fact that most small children spend more time during their early years with their mothers than they do with their fathers.

Nancy Chodorow has done some illuminating work in this area. She points out that a little boy soon realizes that he is not like his mother and that he must differentiate himself from this person. Masculinity is defined by separation. A girl, on the other hand, feels no such need and remains close to her mother. These facts have great consequences for the way we cope when we become adults. Males often grow up being good at independence, but having trouble with closeness. Females often grow up being good at relationship, but having problems with independence.
5. HOW DO YOU REACT TO CONFLICTS? REACTIONS ARE REARED BEHAVIOURS

People react to conflicts differently, some calmly and others with an explosive response. Some people flee from the conflict, and others come back fighting. Some individuals look for ways to negotiate, while others keep pushing to get their own way. Just as conflicts come in many forms, so do our reactions.

Often the way we react to conflicts is also based on how we experienced conflicts growing up. Most likely, today’s reactions are based on yesterday’s model. As you were growing up, how did those around you deal with conflicts?
What messages did your parents, teachers, religious leaders and scoutmasters give you?

Our reactions to conflicts were learned early in our lives. These patterns are well ingrained into our adult behaviour and attitudes. Fortunately we can re-learn and modify the way we react to conflicts.

Reviewing the ways you react to conflict is another piece of the puzzle for understanding how conflicts work. Often a heightened awareness of how we react can help to keep some conflicts from escalating; we can choose how we react. We can actually learn new and better ways to react when we have conflicts.
